Merrimack County, No. 217-2019-CR-01170 STATE OF NEW HAMPSHIRE v. CHRISTOPHER VINCENT

Annotate this Case


Download PDF



					STATE OF NEW HAMPSHIRE SUPERIOR COURT Merrimack, ss. STATE OF NEW HAMPSHIRE Clerk's Notice of Decision Document Sent to Parties on 05/28/2021 v. CHRISTOPHER VINCENT CR 217-2019-CV-01170 ORDER (Regarding Google Records) The matter before the court is the defendant’s motion in limine to exclude electronic records from Google, Inc. Those records purport to show that (a) multiple Google search queries relating to the alleged arson were made on certain dates, and (b)those search queries were made by a user who was, at the time of the search queries, signed into Google under an account allegedly associated with the defendant. The significance of the Google search queries is that they were made long before the defendant became a suspect and long before he was first contacted by law enforcement. Further the search queries were made over the course of several months. The State claims that the Google records are selfauthenticating under N.H.R.Ev. 902(11) because they are accompanied by the required certificate. The defense disagrees and argues the following syllogism: Major Premise: The black letter text of Rule 902(11) only applies to records that meet the requirements of N.H.R.Ev. 803(6)(A)(B) and (C) relating to business records. Minor Premise: The Google records are not do not meet the requirements of 803(6)(A) because they were not created by someone with knowledge (or from information transmitted by someone with knowledge). Conclusion: The Google records are not self-authenticating under Rule 902(11) and the State must call an appropriate witness to authenticate the records. The defense also argues that the records are not relevant under Rules 401 and 402 because there is no evidence linking the defendant to the search search queries. Legal Analysis 1. Authentication The application of Rule 902(11) to electronically generated records presents issues of New Hampshire law that are— surprisingly— unresolved. In this respect, New Hampshire is several years behind the curve. Some months after New Hampshire’s Rule 902 was last amended in 2017, the parallel federal the Rule was amended to add F.R.Ev. 902(13) and (14). Those new federal rules, adopted verbatim in several states, provide for the self-authentication of “certified records generated by an electronic process or system” and “certified data copies from an electronic device, storage medium or file.” These new federal rules dispense with the requirement of calling a sheparding witness to prove that (a) electronic records from Google came from its servers and are accurate and complete copies and (b) those records were generated by an electronic process of system that keeps track of search queries made by users who are signed into to Google accounts The Advisory Committee’s notes to F.R.Ev. 902(13) and (14) are worth quoting in at length (albeit in part): Paragraph (13): The amendment sets forth a procedure by which parties can authenticate certain electronic evidence other than through the testimony of a foundation witness. As with the provisions on business records in Rules 902(11) and (12), the Committee has found that the expense and inconvenience of producing a witness to authenticate an item of electronic evidence is often unnecessary. It is often the case that a party goes to the expense of producing an authentication witness, and then the adversary either stipulates authenticity before the witness is called or fails to challenge the authentication testimony once it is presented. The amendment provides a procedure under which the parties can determine in advance of trial whether a real challenge to authenticity will be made, and can then plan accordingly. * * * A proponent establishing authenticity under this Rule must present a certification containing information that would be sufficient to establish authenticity were that information provided by a witness at trial. If the certification provides information that would be insufficient to authenticate the record if the certifying person testified, then authenticity is not established under this Rule. The Rule specifically allows the authenticity foundation that satisfies Rule 901(b)(9) to be established by a certification rather than the testimony of a live witness. The reference to the "certification requirements of Rule 902(11) or (12)" is only to the procedural requirements for a valid certification. There is no intent to require, or permit, a certification under this Rule to prove the requirements of Rule 803(6). Rule 902(13) is solely limited to authentication, and any attempt to satisfy a hearsay exception must be made independently. A certification under this Rule can establish only that the proffered item has satisfied the admissibility requirements for authenticity. The opponent remains free to object to admissibility of the proffered item on other grounds—including hearsay, relevance, or in criminal cases the right to confrontation. For example, assume that a plaintiff in a defamation case offers what purports to be a printout of a webpage on which a defamatory statement was made. Plaintiff offers a certification under this Rule in which a qualified person describes the process by which the web page was retrieved. Even if that certification sufficiently establishes that the webpage is authentic, defendant remains free to object that the statement on the webpage was not placed there by defendant. Similarly, a certification authenticating a computer output, such as a spreadsheet, does not preclude an objection that the information produced is unreliable—the authentication establishes only that the output came from the computer. A challenge to the authenticity of electronic evidence may require technical information about the system or process at issue, including possibly retaining a forensic technical expert; such factors will affect whether the opponent has a fair opportunity to challenge the evidence given the notice provided. * * * Paragraph (14). The amendment sets forth a procedure by which parties can authenticate data copied from an electronic device, storage medium, or an electronic file, other than through the testimony of a foundation witness. As with the provisions on business records in Rules 902(11) and (12), the Committee has found that the expense and inconvenience of producing an authenticating witness for this evidence is often unnecessary. It is often the case that a party goes to the expense of producing an authentication witness, and then the adversary either stipulates authenticity before the witness is called or fails to challenge the authentication testimony once it is presented. The amendment provides a procedure in which the parties can determine in advance of trial whether a real challenge to authenticity will be made, and can then plan accordingly. Today, data copied from electronic devices, storage media, and electronic files are ordinarily authenticated by "hash value". A hash value is a number that is often represented as a sequence of characters and is produced by an algorithm based upon the digital contents of a drive, medium, or file. If the hash values for the original and copy are different, then the copy is not identical to the original. If the hash values for the original and copy are the same, it is highly improbable that the original and copy are not identical. Thus, identical hash values for the original and copy reliably attest to the fact that they are exact duplicates. This amendment allows self-authentication by a certification of a qualified person that she checked the hash value of the proffered item and that it was identical to the original. The rule is flexible enough to allow certifications through processes other than comparison of hash value, including by other reliable means of identification provided by future technology. * * * See also Facciola & Barrett, Law of the Foal: Careful Steps Towards Digital Competence in Proposed Rules 902(13) and 902(14), 1 Geo. L. Tech. Rev. 6 (2016); Lampley, Something Old and Something New: Exploring the Recent Amendments to the Federal Rules of Evidence, 57 Washburn L.J. 519 (2018); Schupanitz & Chou Lem, Judges' Treatment of Federal Rules of Evidence 902(13) and 902(14), 68 DOJ J. Fed. L. & Prac. 109 (2020). Prior to the adoption of F.R.Ev. 902(13) and (14), the federal courts struggled with the question of whether and when such data could be made self-authenticating through a certification issued under F.R.Ev. 902(11). The difficulty with Rule 902(11) is that it applies only to records that are substantively admissible under the hearsay exception for business (or organization) records. F.R.Ev. 803(6). That hearsay exception requires proof that a person with knowledge created the record for the business. See, e.g., United States v. v. Shah, 125 F. Supp. 3d 570, 575 (E.D.N.C. 2015). Various federal Circuit and District Courts reached disparate results: -In Shah, the U.S. District Court found that emails maintained by Google in a user’s Gmail account could not be authenticated by certification under Rule 902(11). The court grounded its ruling on the fact that the statements in the emails were not Google’s business records. -A more nuanced approach with respect to emails was taken by the Fifth Circuit in United States v. Ayelotan, 917 F.3d 394, 402-403 (5th Cir. 2019). In that case the court noted that Google and Yahoo! emails consisted of two parts (a) a transmittal certificate that recorded the date, time, sending and receiving email accounts and (b) the text of the email. The court treated the transmittal certificate as a business record, because it was automatically created in the ordinary course of business (even though there was no person with knowledge involved). Therefore, the provenance of the emails could be authenticated be certificate under Rule 902(11). The substance of the emails, however, had to be analyzed separately. -The same reasoning was adopted by the Third Circuit in United States v. Browne, 834 F.3d 403 (3d Cir. 2016). In Browne the court held that Facebook chat logs are not business records under F.R.Ev. 803(6)(A)-(C) because Facebook does not ensure reliability of what is said by its users. Therefore, the court ruled that Facebook chat logs cannot be authenticated by certification under Rule 902(11). However, the court went on to opined that, “If the Government here had sought to authenticate only the timestamps on the Facebook chats, the fact that the chats took place between particular Facebook accounts, and similarly technical information verified by Facebook ‘in the course of a regularly conducted activity,’ the records might be more readily analogized to bank records or phone records conventionally authenticated and admitted under Rules 902(11) and 803(6).”). -In United States v. Hassan, 742 F.3d 104, 133–34 (4th Cir. 2014) the U.S. Court of Appeals held that Rule 902(11) allowed for authentication of Facebook pages and YouTube videos by certificate. See also United States v. Camez, 2013 WL 6158402, at *1 (D. Nev. Nov. 21, 2013) (Holding that while Gmail communications may be authenticated by certificate under Rule 902(11), they may alternatively, and at the proponent’s election, certified by testimony from a record-keeper). This court believes that the approach taken by Browne and Ayelotan is generally correct. To the extent that Google has certified that the records in question (a) come from its servers, (b) are search queries made from a device logged into a particular Google account, (c) were made on particular dates and times, and (d) if the records show, from particular locations or devices, the records are self-authenticating under N.H. Rule 902(11). To be sure, N.H.R.Ev. 902(11) is a tight fit because no human with knowledge created the business records. But the same would be true these days for debit card records—there is clearly no human being who creates a record for a purchase of $1.25 Diet Coke by debit card at a particular location on a particular date. Yet, bank records are the quintessential business records. The same would be true for EZ Pass records, phone company connect records, electric meter charges or any number of other records that are now created by computer processes and systems and stored electronically. The court is confronted with only two options: One option is to read 902(11) liberally, in a way that conforms to day-today practice. The other option is to exclude important evidence because the State did not fly in a witness from Mountainview California who could inform the jury that Google stores our data. The court reads the rule liberally to do justice. 2. Relevance The State must do more than merely authenticate the Google search queries. It must connect those queries to the defendant. Although the court held two mid-trial hearings on this issue, the court is still not entirely clear on how the State plans to lay the foundation to connect the defendant with the specific search queries. The court has provided some oral guidance to the State but cannot definitively rule on the issue until either (a) the evidence is presented or (b) a more fulsome offer of proof is made. 3. Conclusion The Google records related to the search queries are selfauthenticated under Rule 902(11) by virtue of the certificate. They will not be admissible, however, until the State lays a proper foundation connecting the search queries to the defendant. May 28, 2021 ___________________________ Andrew R. Schulman, Presiding Justice
